title: John Cage’s most famous piece has no notes, and it isn’t silent
body: 4′33″, composed by John Cage in 1952, tells the performer not to play for three movements. At the premiere on 29 August 1952 in Woodstock, New York, pianist David Tudor sat at the keyboard while, as Cage recalled, the wind stirred outside, raindrops hit the roof and people talked or walked out. In an anechoic chamber at Harvard, Cage had expected silence and instead heard two sounds, one high and one low; the engineer told him they were his nervous system and his blood in circulation. His conclusion: **there is no such thing as silence**, and the piece makes an audience hear what it usually ignores.

slides.text: What they thought was silence, because they didn’t know how to listen, was full of accidental sounds.

slides.prompt: How did Tudor show where each ‘silent’ movement began and ended?
slides.answer: He closed the piano lid to start and briefly reopened it at each movement’s end
slides.detail: The Woodstock score gives the movements as 30 seconds, 2 minutes 23 seconds and 1 minute 40 seconds.

slides.heading: The anechoic chamber
slides.text: In 1951 Cage visited an anechoic chamber at Harvard, a room built to absorb all sound. He heard two sounds, one high and one low. The engineer told him the high one was his nervous system in operation and the low one his blood in circulation.

slides.question: How long are the three movements, as given in the Woodstock score?
options: 4 min 33 s, then two of 0 s
slides.explanation: Thirty seconds, 2 minutes 23 seconds and 1 minute 40 seconds, which add up to the 4 minutes 33 seconds of the title.
